newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian president waives taxes to help investors.
newsitem.headline: Albanian president waives taxes to help investors.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha said on Tuesday he was removing all taxes for two years for residents in this region to help them recover after losing large sums of money to fraudulent pyramid investment schemes.

"I ordered the finance minister to lift taxes for two years in Lushnje to help farmers and citizens out of this crisis," he said in the southern town which was swept by rioting after the get-rich-quick schemes collapsed in January.

Berisha entered the local theatre to applause and chants of "Sali Berisha" but he was booed by a number of onlookers in the streets when he left 90 minutes later. A rock was hurled at his car as he drove off, one eyewitness said.

Police imposed heavy security for his visit. Plainclothes police swarmed over the town centre. Armed guards were perched on rooftops overlooking the main square and police told drivers they could not park nearby.
"I have come not only to meet you but all Lushnje people," he told a meeting of selected supporters. "I share the concern of all investors who lost their money in the pyramid schemes."
Before entering the theatre, he broke with security and waded into a crowd of some 2,000 people, shaking hands and expressing his interest in their plight.
"We'll do our best to solve the problem but Albanians must also accept their responsibility in this," he said as he moved through the crowd.

Berisha launched his campaign to win back popular support on Saturday, candidly telling Albanians he had made mistakes in handling the pyramid scandal but also saying investors bore the main responsibility for putting their money in risky ventures.
He worked the same theme in his address to supporters at the Lushnje theatre.
"I came to you to admit errors and mistakes by the ruling goverment, the party and by me," he said. "But I am open and I can tell you the people are also to blame."
He again expressed his anger at those in Lushnje who beat up Deputy Prime Minister Tritan Shehu when he came to discuss the pyramid collapse in January.

"I have never lost confidence in you, that is why I sent Mr. Shehu here to talk to you," he said. "But unfortunately a group of adventurers tried to take him hostage. I would award medals to those who saved him."
Facing a month of nationwide riots and protests, Berisha appealed for people to remember what Albania was like just five years ago after 45 years under a ruthless Stalinist regime.
"I understand we are talking about big losses. But do not forget what your lives were like five years ago. Now you are four times better than you were then," he said.
Berisha trotted out a string of promises for Lushnje, from declaring it a free trade zone to speeding privatisation of industry, petrol and telecommunications.

He even promised to help out the local soccer team, drawing huge applause from the audience. The Lushnje club was sponsored by Pellumb Xhaferri, the detained chief manager of one of the collapsed pyramid schemes.
Thousands of investors blame the pro-market government for failing to regulate the schemes, which lured cash with offers of high interest, and failing to warn them of the risks.

Albanians pumped an estimated $1 to $2 billion dollars into the schemes, which offered interest of 60 percent or more a month. Five schemes collapsed in January and four investment holding companies froze clients' accounts.
The ruling Democrats, who espouse free market economics, were elected in 1992 and were re-elected to a four-year term last year.

They are facing their worst crisis. Thousands of investors are demanding compensation and have called for the government to resign. Police have been enforcing strict security and have stopped opposition rallies in Tirana.
